Coverage and enrichment testing

coverage_and_enrichment.Rmd

Overview

Among other things, the multifactor package provides a set of tools to calculate coverage and estimate enrichment for relational datasets. This type of operation forms the basis for bioinformatics techniques such as pathway enrichment analysis (PEA), but have application far beyond the biological sciences.

Setup 

library(multifactor)

# Wrangling
library(dplyr)

# Plotting
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(systemfonts)
library(ragg)

# Define utility function
split_to_letters <- function(x) unique(
  unlist(
    strsplit(gsub(" ", "", x), split = ""),
    recursive = TRUE, use.names = FALSE
  )
)

Example Dataset: The Quick Brown Fox

We will use a toy data set of hierarchically structured data, namely the sentence: ‘The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.’ This sentence is a pangram, meaning that all 26 letters of the English alphabet are represented. Moreover, we have deconstructed the sentence to three levels; letters, words and constituents.

# Load the quick brown fox data set
set.seed(2612)
fox <- quickbrownfox()

We could represent these relations visually like so:

We can convince ourselves this same information is captured in the multifactor object, fox.

levels(fox)
#> $letter
#>  [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n" "o" "p" "q" "r" "s"
#> [20] "t" "u" "v" "w" "x" "y" "z"
#> 
#> $word
#> [1] "brown" "dog"   "fox"   "jumps" "lazy"  "over"  "quick" "the"  
#> 
#> $constituent
#> [1] "object"    "predicate" "subject"  
#> 
#> $sentence
#> [1] "complete pangram"

as.matrix(fox$letter2word)
#> 26 x 8 sparse Matrix of class "ngCMatrix"

Calculate coverage

With coverage, we mean the proportion of items in a set that are present. In other words, going back to our example, given some number of letters, we can calculate which words we can make, and how complete they are.

To demonstrate, we’ll need to generate some collection of letters as input data:

# Generate some collection of letters
input <- split_to_letters("some collection of letters")

input
#>  [1] "s" "o" "m" "e" "c" "l" "t" "i" "n" "f" "r"

We can use the weave_coverage() function to calculate to what degree the input letters cover the words in our data set. This function behaves similarly to weave() but comes with an additional argument, .data. For now, let’s plug in our input letters:

res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input
)

as.data.frame(res)
#>    letter  word observed set_count set_size  coverage complete
#> 1       t   the     TRUE         2        3 0.6666667    FALSE
#> 2       h   the    FALSE         2        3 0.6666667    FALSE
#> 3       e   the     TRUE         2        3 0.6666667    FALSE
#> 4       q quick    FALSE         2        5 0.4000000    FALSE

#> 6       i quick     TRUE         2        5 0.4000000    FALSE

#> 8       k quick    FALSE         2        5 0.4000000    FALSE

Now, let’s use a second set of letters that are explicitly part of the sentence:

input <- split_to_letters("jumps over")

input

res <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input

Notice that the column named "complete" marks two particular words as complete now.

We can use the subset() method for linkmap to automatically filter for complete cases:

subset(res)
#> A multifactor::linkmap data.frame S7_object: 9 rows.
#>   letter  word
#> 1      j jumps
#> 2      u jumps
#> 3      m jumps
#> 4      p jumps
#> 5      s jumps
#> 6      o  over
#> 7      v  over
#> 8      e  over
#> 9      r  over
#> 
#> @ levels:   2 variables: 
#>  $ letter : 26 Levels: a ... z 
#>  $ word   :  8 Levels: brown ... the 
#> 
#> @ metadata: 5 variables: 
#> List of 5
#>  $ observed : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ...
#>  $ set_count: int  5 5 5 5 5 4 4 4 4
#>  $ set_size : int  5 5 5 5 5 4 4 4 4
#>  $ coverage : num  1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1
#>  $ complete : logi  TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE ...

Enrichment testing

The test_enrich() allows for quick hypothesis testing using the same syntax:

test_enrich(x = fox, .path = letter ~ word, .data = input)
#>        expected  observed      fold    log_fold     p.value      p.adj
#> brown 0.3461538 0.4000000 1.1555556  0.20858662 0.580297963 0.98461538
#> dog   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538
#> fox   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538
#> jumps 0.3461538 1.0000000 2.8888889  1.53051472 0.001915476 0.01532381
#> lazy  0.3461538 0.0000000 0.0000000        -Inf 1.000000000 1.00000000
#> over  0.3461538 1.0000000 2.8888889  1.53051472 0.008428094 0.03371237
#> quick 0.3461538 0.2000000 0.5777778 -0.79141338 0.905928854 1.00000000
#> the   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538

Alternatively, test_enrich() can also be run on the result of an earlier weave_coverage() call for the same results:

test_enrich(res)
#>        expected  observed      fold    log_fold     p.value      p.adj
#> brown 0.3461538 0.4000000 1.1555556  0.20858662 0.580297963 0.98461538
#> dog   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538
#> fox   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538
#> jumps 0.3461538 1.0000000 2.8888889  1.53051472 0.001915476 0.01532381
#> lazy  0.3461538 0.0000000 0.0000000        -Inf 1.000000000 1.00000000
#> over  0.3461538 1.0000000 2.8888889  1.53051472 0.008428094 0.03371237
#> quick 0.3461538 0.2000000 0.5777778 -0.79141338 0.905928854 1.00000000
#> the   0.3461538 0.3333333 0.9629630 -0.05444778 0.738461538 0.98461538

Defining coverage

By default, coverage is only calculated between the data types involved in the last step of the path:

path <- select_path(fox, letter ~ constituent)
path
#> A multifactor::path_frame S7_object.
#>   A path from `letter` to `constituent`:
#> letter ~ word ~ constituent
#> 
#>     from          to cov_operator cov_value stack components
#> 1 letter        word           >=         0 FALSE          1
#> 2   word constituent           >=         0 FALSE          1

input_full <- split_to_letters("jumps over")
input_no_r <- split_to_letters("jumps ove")

res_full <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ constituent, .data = input_full
)

res_no_r <- weave_coverage(
  x = fox, .path = letter ~ constituent, .data = input_no_r
)

as.data.frame(res_full)
